Correlations

Source: vignettes/articles/correlations.qmd 
library(apa7)
library(dplyr)
library(flextable)
library(ftExtra)
library(tidyr)
library(stringr)
library(correlation)
apa7_defaults(font_family = "Open Sans", line_spacing = 1.5)

Correlation matrices look simple enough…until you try to make one by hand in MS Word. The apa_cor function can remove most of the tedium by formatting most of what can automated, and any finishing touches can be added with a styling function.

The examples use the epi.bfi data set from the psychTools package (Revelle, 2019), which has personality, depression, and anxiety scores for 231 participants in studies at Northwestern University’s Personality, Motivation, and Cognition Laboratory. Openness, conscientiousness, extraversion, agreeableness, and neuroticism are Big Five scale scores, and depression is the Beck Depression Inventory score.

d_personality <- psychTools::epi.bfi |>
  select(
    Openness = bfopen,
    Conscientiousness = bfcon,
    Extraversion = bfext,
    Agreeablness = bfagree,
    Neuroticism = bfneur,
    Depression = bdi
  )

By default, the output of apa_cor flextable, with significant correlations starred.

d_personality |> 
  apa_cor()

Significant correlations can be bolded instead.

d_personality |>
  apa_cor(bold_significant = TRUE)

Summary functions

You can include any named list of summary functions:

# Named list of descriptive functions
my_summaries <- list(Mdn = median, "*IQR*" = IQR)

apa_cor(d_personality, 
        summary_functions = my_summaries, 
        star_significant = FALSE)

You can also use a plain vector of descriptive functions from these options: "IQR", "Interquartile Range", "Kurtosis", "MAD", "Median Absolute Deviation", "M", "Mean", "Med", "Median", "n", "N", "Quantile", "Range", "SD", "Skewness", "Var", "Variance"

my_summaries <- c("n", "M", "SD", "Skewness", "Kurtosis")

apa_cor(d_personality, summary_functions = my_summaries)

Styling options

Your styling options include:

  • note A custom markdown formatted note. Overrides automatic note about bolded correlations being significant. Default: NULL
  • p_value Significance value. Default: 0.05
  • digits Number of digits for rounding. Default: 2
  • bold_significant Whether to bold significant correlations. Default: FALSE
  • star_significant Whether to star significant correlations. Default: TRUE
  • significance_note Whether note about bolding correlations appears. Overridden by a custom note. Also, the automatic note will not appear if no correlations are significant. Default: TRUE
  • output Options are flextable or tibble. Default: flextable
  • family Font family (typeface). Default: Times New Roman
  • font_size Font size (in points). Default: 12
  • text_color Text color. Default: black
  • border_color Table border color. Default: black
  • border_width Table border width. Default: 0.5
  • line_spacing Text line spacing. Default: 2

For example,

d_personality |>
  apa_cor(
    p_value = 0.001,
    digits = 2,
    bold_significant = TRUE,
    significance_note = TRUE,
    summary_functions = my_summaries,
    font_family = "Arial",
    font_size = 10,
    text_color = "darkred",
    border_color = "royalblue4",
    border_width = 1,
    line_spacing = 2
  )

To remove summary statistics entirely, set summary_functions to NA or NULL.

apa_cor(d_personality, summary_functions = NA)

Customization

The styling options for apa_cor are minimal, but flextable allows for all kinds of customization. Just place whatever code from flextable you want after apa_cor. Here I set the width to 50% and align the table to the left of the page. I place a footnote in a specific cell in the table body.

apa_cor(d_personality, table_width = .5) |>
  flextable::footnote(
    i = 2,
    j = "Variable",
    value = flextable::as_paragraph("This is a footnote."),
    part = "body"
  )

Output to tibble

If you need to process the underlying data before converting to flextable (or use another table-creating function from another package), you can output a tibble and then process the table however you want. Here we add a row title.

apa_cor(d_personality, output = "tibble") |>
  mutate(apa7listcolumn = str_trim(apa7listcolumn)) |>
  unite(col = Variable, 
        apa7listcolumn, 
        Variable, 
        sep = "&thinsp;") |>
  add_row(Variable = "Row title", .before = 1) |>
  apa_flextable(no_format_columns = "Variable") |>
  padding(i = 2:7,
          j = 1,
          padding.left = 15)

Other Kinds of Correlations

apa_cor computes the correlations with correlation::correlation from the correlation package: by default, Pearson correlations with unadjusted p-values. Depression scores are skewed, as the skewness in the summary statistics above shows, so rank correlations are a reasonable alternative. The method argument chooses the kind of correlation. For example, Spearman rank correlations:

apa_cor(d_personality, method = "spearman")

The note says what kind of correlations are shown. Other options for method include:

Option Correlation
pearson Pearson’s Correlation (default)
spearman Spearman’s Rank Correlation
kendall Kendall’s Rank Correlation
biserial Biserial Correlation
polychoric Polychoric Correlation
tetrachoric Tetrachoric Correlation
biweight Biweight midcorrelation
distance Distance Correlation
percentage Percentage Bend Correlation
blomqvist Blomqvist’s coefficient
hoeffding Hoeffding’s D
gamma Gamma Correlation
gaussian for Gaussian Rank correlation
shepherd for Shepherd’s Pi correlation

To adjust the p-values (and so the stars) for multiple comparisons, use p_adjust (e.g., p_adjust = "holm"), and the note says how they were adjusted. Partial correlations, each controlling for the other variables in the table, need only partial = TRUE:

apa_cor(d_personality, partial = TRUE)

Partial correlations can differ considerably from ordinary correlations. With zero-order correlations, openness and extraversion correlate at .27, but once other personality variables are held constant, the partial correlation between them is close to zero.

Other arguments of correlation::correlation (e.g., robust = TRUE, winsorize = .2, or multilevel = TRUE) can be given to apa_cor as well. Variable names with spaces work for every kind of correlation, because apa_cor gives the variables internal names while it computes the correlations. (Called directly, correlation::correlation does not accept such names for partial or multilevel correlations.)

The output of correlation::correlation can also be given to apa_cor:

correlation(d_personality, method = "spearman") |>
  apa_cor()

Here, correlation::correlation adjusted the p-values with Holm’s method, its default, so the stars are for the adjusted p-values, and the note says so. The means and standard deviations come from the data that correlation::correlation keeps with its results. Correlations computed by group, between two sets of variables, or with Bayesian methods are not yet supported.

References

Holm, S. (1979). A simple sequentially rejective multiple test procedure. Scandinavian Journal of Statistics, 6(2), 65–70. https://www.jstor.org/stable/4615733
Revelle, W. (2019). psychTools: Tools to accompany the psych package for psychological research (Version 2.6.4) [Computer software]. Comprehensive R Archive Network. https://doi.org/10.32614/CRAN.package.psychTools
